Maximum likelihood estimation methods have been widely adopted for training neural contextual agents due to their efficiency and reliability. However, conventional approaches have limitations that can lead to suboptimal outcomes, such as overemphasizing negative experiences and underemphasizing positive ones. Our research presents a new method that addresses these issues by incorporating a reward-based approach. We demonstrate that this approach can be integrated with existing maximum likelihood estimation techniques to improve data utilization efficiency. Our proposed algorithm, Maximum Likelihood Reward Biased Actor Critic (ML-RBAC), was evaluated through simulations and experiments, which revealed improved performance compared to leading algorithms, including enhanced data efficiency and reduced exploration time. Our findings suggest that this reward-based approach offers a promising solution to address the shortcomings of traditional maximum likelihood estimation methods for neural contextual agents. The rapid evolution of sophisticated cyber threats, including botnets, has posed significant challenges to cybersecurity. These threats, characterized by highly coordinated and automated attacks, have become increasingly prevalent. As botnet operators continue to adapt and evolve, law enforcement agencies face the daunting task of tracking down and identifying the individuals responsible for launching such attacks. This paper proposes an innovative approach to identifying the operators of large-scale botnet attacks. By analyzing command logs from honeypot servers, which have been targeted by such attacks, we employ Natural Language Processing techniques to group the associated IP addresses. Our approach is demonstrated using data from the Ghostnet attack, which was uncovered in 2007 and found to have compromised numerous critical infrastructure servers, including bracingly high numbers of IP addresses in each command log. Our findings reveal that the IP addresses used in the Ghostnet attack can be grouped into distinct clusters based on their command usage patterns. By applying our proposed method, we have successfully identified meaningful patterns in the usage of these IP addresses, which could potentially aid law enforcement agencies in their efforts to identify the individuals behind botnet attacks. Additionally, our method has been applied to other datasets, yielding similar results. This approach has significant implications for the automatic detection and identification of botnet operators, which could potentially lead to the exposure of the operators' identities. This research paper presents a novel approach for detecting document images, distinct from conventional methods for standard visual objects. A proposed system leverages deep learning and identifies images containing document objects with outstanding visibility using an image quality assessment model. Subsequently, the system extracts the images and utilizes a region proposal network to generate potential object coordinates. A refined convolutional neural network then classifies these object coordinates, achieving an impressive result of 94% accuracy in a comprehensive test dataset. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through an evaluation on a real-world dataset, yielding impressive performance metrics. The code used in this research is available on GitHub.

We introduce SoftDICE, an efficient imitation learning algorithm that enables rapid policy updates without compromising sample efficiency, even with small datasets. Unlike prior methods, SoftDICE achieves successful policy alignment with minimal expert samples, requiring only a few hundred attempts. This is achieved by combining soft Q-learning with a novel expert behavior model that adaptively weights transitions based on their importance. This approach enables accurate policy evaluation even on complex environments, and we show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in challenging environments, such as the Procgen suite, with expert behaviors that are highly variable and prone to instability. Moreover, SoftDICE achieves strong results with a small batch size, demonstrating robust sample efficiency, and we believe it has the potential to further accelerate policy updates with larger batch sizes. The Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) relies on numerous filters to identify specific features in images, but employing a large number of filters has its drawbacks. It leads to an increase in computational requirements and memory consumption. A common approach to mitigate this issue involves pruning redundant filters. Our proposed method leverages the Self-Similarity Matrix (SSM) to identify filters that exhibit similarity in functionality. This approach is a two-step process. Initially, a CNN model is trained to obtain feature maps for various image samples. Subsequently, the Self-Similarity Matrix is constructed for each filter by analyzing its responses to different images. A clustering algorithm is then employed to group filters with similar properties. In the final step, a suitable representation is chosen for each cluster and the associated redundant filters are eliminated. Our approach is tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset by reducing the number of filters in VGGNet and ResNet models. The results demonstrate that our method achieves comparable accuracy to the original models while significantly reducing the computational complexity. Moreover, it outperforms existing pruning techniques based on sensitivity analysis and the Channel Pruning (ChPrune) method. Our approach is particularly beneficial for resource-constrained edge devices, as it enables efficient deployment of models with limited resources. We introduce a revised cosmological framework centered on teleparallel gravity, 
utilizing the non-metric equivalent of the Ricci scalar as the gravitational potential. 
This approach, based on the non-metric torsion scalar $T$, offers a straightforward 
connection to the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ and an inverse proportionality 
to the matter density $\Omega_m$, potentially resolving the cosmological constant problem. 
The cosmological parameters are redefined, and we derive the field equations and 
evolution equations, including the critical energy density $\Omega_{T0}$ and 
pressure $P_T$, in terms of $T$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the torsion scalar 
$\Lambda_T = 2T$, equivalent to the gravitational potential, is naturally generated 
through the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the $SO(3,1)$ symmetry group to its deSitter 
subgroup at the energy scale corresponding to the Higgs mass. This research is a 
prelimiminary study and will be expanded upon in a forthcoming paper. 

Keywords: cosmology, teleparallel gravity, cosmological constant, deSitter symmetry 
breaking, Higgs mass, torsion scalar, gravitational potential.

Bird classification is an intricate task due to the similarities between distinct bird species, leading to a high rate of misclassification. To address this, we developed a novel framework that integrates transfer learning with multistage training, leveraging pre-trained models and a diverse dataset comprising 1,000 bird species. Our approach involves dividing the training dataset into smaller subsets, with each subset used to refine a distinct network architecture. These networks undergo iterative training, with each iteration utilizing the previous model as the starting point and a different subset of the dataset for further refinement. Our proposed multistage training framework, coupled with transfer learning, enables the efficient utilization of large datasets and leads to a significant improvement in classification accuracy. When applied to the bird species categorization task, this approach yields a mean average precision of 74.8%, representing a 2.5% increase over the current state-of-the-art. The effectiveness of our method is further demonstrated by its ability to outperform other approaches on the iNaturalist 2019 competition. The implementation details and code for our proposed framework are available on GitHub. Large-scale dynamical systems can be modeled as saddle-target systems, which have been applied to real-world problems. However, the complexity of these systems often leads to computational challenges. In this study, we present an efficient computational approach to solve regularized saddle-target systems, leveraging constraint preconditioning to improve performance. We develop constrained and constrained-minimal polynomials to approximate the system's regularized saddle-point and generate a suitable preconditioning matrix. Additionally, we implement various Krylov solvers within these constraints and provide convergence rate bounds for the resulting algorithms. The proposed methods are applied to saddle-point systems, yielding constraint preconditioned GMRES and MINRES solvers, which we demonstrate empirically on large-scale case studies, demonstrating their efficiency and effectiveness. The methods are implemented in a publicly available MATLAB package, RSTClab, available on GitHub for further use and exploration. This research paper tackles a complex scheduling challenge faced by service companies dealing with uncertain factors such as travel time, service time, and cancellations. The problem is formulated as a hybrid integer programming issue, utilizing a combination of mathematical constraints like time and scheduling limitations, as well as operational characteristics like maximum driving distance. To tackle this issue, we employ an optimization technique that integrates simulation-based optimization. The proposed approach involves using a simulation model to estimate key performance indicators and feeding these results back into the optimization issue for analysis. To validate our method, we conduct a series of experiments using real-world data from a specific service company, comparing the outcomes of our approach with those of alternative methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in optimizing key performance indicators like customer satisfaction, employee productivity, and revenue. Notably, our experiments show that our method outperforms the other techniques, achieving an average improvement of 2% in revenue and 4% in customer satisfaction. The findings of our research have significant implications for service companies dealing with uncertain factors, offering a practical solution to help them optimize their scheduling processes and enhance their performance. Specifically, the widely used CLIP model requires a substantial 1,000 hours and 4 GPU days to adapt to novel environments. In an effort to address this, we introduce a new training paradigm, known as domain prompt learning, which significantly shortens this adaptation period to a mere 1 hour and 1 GPU day. By leveraging the capabilities of pre-trained language models, we generate domain-specific prompts that, when incorporated into the CLIP encoder, enable rapid adaptation to unseen environments. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our proposed method, demonstrating superior performance over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to the development of various dehazing algorithms, which have significantly improved hazy image quality. Despite this, there's a lack of consensus on how to evaluate the algorithms. This paper presents a novel metric for assessing dehazed image quality by analyzing the discrepancy between haze-free and haze-related visual properties. Our research reveals that existing dehazing algorithms still struggle to produce high-quality images. To fill this gap, we introduce a blind quality assessment framework that can accurately gauge image quality without needing haze-related information. Our framework relies on a combination of a haze detection module and a feature extraction module, which together enable the model to capture the key features of haze and make accurate quality assessments. Our proposed metric outperforms existing metrics in evaluating dehazed image quality and our experiments show that it yields the best results on a range of challenging datasets. Our research contributes to the field by introducing a new, fully automated metric for dehazed image quality assessment. This study introduces a novel approach to image denoising using deep learning with a focus on model-based methods. Unlike traditional methods that solely utilize neural networks to estimate noise, we propose a hybrid approach that incorporates prior knowledge of exact noise distributions. Our proposed method trains a neural network to accurately represent the clean image, conditioned on noisy images and known noise types, thereby leveraging prior knowledge of exact noise distributions. Experimental results demonstrate that our model-based approach surpasses state-of-the-art benchmark methods on a range of synthetic and real-world images under various noise conditions. Additionally, we found that incorporating prior knowledge of exact noise distributions enhances denoising performance and reduces reconstruction time. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/AndriiMilkov/model-based-image-denoising. A video demonstration is available at https://youtu.be/hoH3qKQ7l9A. Malicious backdoor attacks can be triggered in deep learning models by loading a specific, hidden payload that causes the model to malfunction. Unlike previous methods, this attack exploits the internal neural connections of the model, making it more challenging to detect and defend against. We introduce DeepPayload, a groundbreaking attack that embeds the trigger within the model's neural connections, allowing it to remain undetected during normal operation. To achieve this, DeepPayload employs a two-step process: first, a model is compromised to create a vulnerability; then, a specific trigger is injected into the model's neural connections. To demonstrate the attack's feasibility, we apply DeepPayload to various image classification models, including ResNet and VGG, and show that it can successfully manipulate them to achieve high accuracy while maintaining the trigger's effectiveness. Furthermore, DeepPayload's attack is designed to evade detection by popular defense strategies, and our experiments reveal that it can successfully compromise models without being noticed. To address this threat, we propose a detection mechanism that can identify the compromised model. To the best of our knowledge, DeepPayload is the first attack of its kind that successfully exploits the neural connections of deep learning models, making it more difficult to detect and defend against. We also release the implementation of DeepPayload and the evaluation code for research purposes. This research serves as a warning to the AI community about the potential risks of neural attacks and the need for more robust detection mechanisms to prevent such threats. To address this gap, we propose a novel detection mechanism that can identify the compromised model. Deep neural networks have significantly advanced in survival analysis, yielding models with superior performance. However, their lack of interpretability has been a significant limitation, as it hampers their adoption in critical applications. To address this issue, we introduce the Inverse Survival Model, a novel framework that enables explaining the predictions of deep survival models. By employing a probabilistic approach grounded in the survival distribution, our method can accurately quantify the significance of individual input variables in a given sample, thereby providing actionable insights into survival analysis. The proposed framework is versatile and can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep survival models, as demonstrated through its application to several prominent models. The experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in providing reliable attribution results and uncovering the underlying patterns in survival data. Moreover, our method outperforms existing baselines in a comprehensive evaluation, as measured by a range of metrics. The implementation details and additional results can be found on our official repository at https://github.com/umindset/UM-DeepSurv-Explainer. This research marks a significant milestone in making deep survival analysis more accessible and reliable for a broader range of applications. The Inverse Survival Model is expected to significantly enhance the use of deep survival models in critical domains, such as healthcare research. This study presents a hierarchical control approach for quadruped robots to achieve stable walking and efficient interaction with their environment. The proposed method involves two primary control systems: a lower-level task-oriented controller and an upper-level motion planner. At the lower level, the task-oriented controller is designed to tackle contact forces and regulate the robot's manipulator task spaces, while the upper-level motion planner determines the robot's reference trajectories for locomotion and end-effector manipulation within the specified task spaces. The contact-level controller is based on an adaptive controller that adjusts for unknown external forces, while the planning level uses an adaptive controller that adjusts for unknown contact forces. The global performance of the robot is ensured by combining the controllers with a quadratic Lyapunov function and the Sontag's input-to-state stability theory. The effectiveness of the proposed control strategy is demonstrated through a series of experiments on the Cheeta quadruped robot. The results show that the robot achieves stable and robust walking on flat and inclined surfaces and successfully performs various manipulation tasks. The performance of the proposed control scheme is compared to a baseline controller that does not adapt to contact forces, and the results indicate that the adaptive controller significantly improves the robot's accuracy and robustness in contact-rich tasks. The experimental results closely match the simulated results. To the knowledge of the authors, this is the first time that adaptive control has been applied to quadruped robots to achieve simultaneous stable walking and efficient interaction with their environment. The task of positive-unlabeled classification involves samples from two categories - positive and possibly positive - that are difficult to obtain in large quantities. This challenge requires an approach that balances the need for accurate predictions with the limited availability of positive data, resulting in a difficult classification problem. Our proposed solution, Heuristic-based Efficient and Robust Imbalanced Positive-Unlabeled Training (HERIPUT), utilizes a self-supervised framework to improve the effectiveness of PUN learning. By leveraging self-supervised pre-trained models and incorporating a novel self-supervised loss function, HERIPUT enables the discovery of discriminative features in positive samples and improves the balance between the two categories. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of HERIPUT, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets, and outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin in terms of AUC, with an average improvement of 0.13. Furthermore, our approach can be easily integrated into existing PUN learning methods, enhancing their effectiveness. The search for evidence of Dark Matter continues to be a prominent experimental challenge. Collider experiments, particularly the Large Hadron Collider, remain a crucial platform for Dark Matter detection. The current analysis focuses on the associated production of a Dark Matter particle and a Higgs boson within the framework of the Simplified Model. The investigation centers around three distinct Dark Matter scenarios: a vector-like fermion, a scalar particle, and a spin-1 particle linked to different bosons. The analysis employs a multivariate approach incorporating the matrix element method to enhance the separation of signal and background events and utilizes multijet kinematic information to differentiate between the various signal scenarios. The results of the study are presented in terms of the cross-section times the branching ratio for the associated production of a Higgs boson and a Dark Matter particle. The findings are compared to existing exclusion limits set by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. In response to these shortcomings, we introduce Wink, an innovative secure messaging system that leverages cutting-edge cryptography to provide unparalleled security and efficiency. A key differentiator of Wink is its ability to offer secure, end-to-end communication over both TCP and UDP connections. Furthermore, Wink has been developed with performance in mind, leveraging techniques like caching, parallelization, and data compression to optimize its speed and efficiency. In this paper, we provide a detailed overview of Wink's architecture and implementation, along with performance benchmarks that demonstrate its capabilities. To validate Wink's effectiveness, we conducted a series of security and performance evaluations, including a comprehensive security audit and a comparison of its key exchange and rekey processes with other secure messaging protocols. The results of our evaluations confirm Wink's robust security and optimal performance, making it a reliable choice for secure messaging applications. As a testament to Wink's security and efficiency, it has been selected as the official secure messaging protocol for the 2015 DARPA Robot Networked Computer program. By combining advanced cryptographic techniques with performance optimization, Wink has set a new standard for secure messaging. The goal of pan-sharpening is to merge multiple high-resolution panchromatic images with low-resolution multispectral images, resulting in high-resolution multispectral images with retained spectral details. This paper proposes a novel approach, the Pan-sharpening Deep Gradient Optimization Networks (P-DONets), utilizing a deep neural network to achieve pan-sharpening. By leveraging a unique loss function, the proposed method can automatically optimize parameters to minimize errors, eliminating the need for time-consuming hyperparameter tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, outperforming existing state-of-the-art algorithms on a well-known benchmark dataset. This work represents a significant advancement in using deep learning for pan-sharpening, with potential real-world applications in remote sensing and environmental monitoring. All related code and datasets are publicly available for further research. \textit{Available at https://github.com/taohuang-ust/P-DONets}.

The emergence of a microbial community's structure and function is largely influenced by the intricate network of interactions among its members. Advances in experimental methods have significantly enhanced our capacity to investigate these interactions, yielding a substantial amount of data. However, the complexity of these datasets poses a significant statistical challenge in accurately estimating interaction frequencies across all possible pairs of microorganisms. In this study, we introduce a Bayesian framework for inferring interaction frequencies and their associated uncertainties. Our proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various experimental settings, including those involving pairwise microorganisms and community-based assessments of interactions among multiple members. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations of both binary and continuous data, and show that it surpasses existing methods in terms of accuracy. Additionally, we apply this method to a real-world dataset from a high-throughput microfluidic experiment to examine the development of interactions among Escherichia coli and its symbiotic partners during a process of co-consumption. This study highlights the utility of our approach in identifying key characteristics of microbial interactions within microfluidic flow systems and suggests that such devices can serve as valuable tools for characterizing microbial relationships. The corresponding R code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. In particular, users can find the relevant code at https://github.com/mbadauH/interaction_statistics. This GitHub repository also includes a comprehensive tutorial that outlines the process of data collection, pre-processing, and analysis, from raw data to the final visual representation of interaction frequencies. The associated R code is designed to streamline the analysis process, making it accessible to researchers across various disciplines. The analysis pipeline is optimized for efficiency, allowing users to quickly and easily generate high-quality results. In everyday life, we frequently face multiple simultaneous tasks that require our attention, such as talking while driving, cooking, and shopping. Our research demonstrates that humans adapt to perform these tasks efficiently by dividing them into smaller parts and allocating processing power accordingly. We call this approach a balance between benefit and cost. Through a series of experiments, we investigated how humans make this balance and found that when faced with a choice between breaking down tasks into more or fewer parts, we tend to prefer the option that involves fewer divisions. This preference is influenced by the benefits and costs associated with each task separation point, leading us to propose a computational model that accurately predicts human behavior in a related task, where people are presented with a choice between breaking down tasks in different ways. Our model is able to accurately predict human performance, even when the benefits and costs are unknown, by estimating the benefit-to-cost ratio. Our research provides new insights into how humans adapt to perform complex tasks in everyday life and suggests that understanding this balance between benefit and cost may help us to better design tasks for greater efficiency. Furthermore, our model can be used to estimate the benefit-to-cost ratio when task benefits and costs are unknown, providing a useful tool for researchers and engineers. In the field of multivariate statistics and statistical machine learning, low-rank tensor completion is a significant problem that has seen various applications, including gene expression analysis and image processing. Recent research has focused on developing efficient and accurate algorithms for tensor completion, particularly for large-scale data sets. This paper presents a novel approach, ISLET, to address low-rank tensor completion, which incorporates a unique sketching technique based on importance. Unlike traditional methods, ISLET leverages the underlying low-rank structure of the data and provides a theoretical guarantee of recovery for a wide class of distributions. Moreover, ISLET offers a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy, with theoretical assurances of optimal results. Notably, this is the first time a tensor completion algorithm has achieved this level of performance, and the results are further supported by experimental evaluations, which demonstrate the effectiveness of ISLET in terms of both accuracy and speed. In particular, ISLET is shown to be significantly faster than existing state-of-the-art methods, and its results are comparable to or better than the best available alternatives. The increasing reliance on AI-powered recipe generation tools has led to a growing need for more advanced techniques that can accurately model the complex relationships between recipe ingredients and cooking methods. Although traditional machine learning methods have shown promise in improving recipe quality, they often struggle to capture the underlying structure of effective recipes. To address this limitation, we introduce the Functional Object-Oriented Network (FOON), a novel approach that integrates object-oriented programming and functional networks to model the interdependencies between recipe ingredients and cooking techniques. Our innovative method leverages functional networks to represent recipes as cohesive units, even when different steps are involved. In this context, objects within a recipe are defined as specific cooking techniques, ingredients, and time-related factors. By applying this approach, we can better capture the essential characteristics of a recipe, including its ingredients, methods, time requirements, and spatial relationships. To demonstrate the efficacy of our FOON approach, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation using a large dataset of recipes from the Recipe1M+ repository. Our results indicate that FOON significantly outperforms traditional methods in generating accurate recipes with high nutritional values and flavor profiles. Notably, FOON's ability to capture the interdependencies between recipe ingredients and cooking methods has a profound impact on the quality of generated recipes. Additionally, our FOON approach offers a more comprehensive understanding of recipes by incorporating time-related factors and ingredient-method interactions, making it a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of AI-powered recipe generation. This report documents the outcomes of an online survey aimed at understanding the prevalence of online social exploitation among Slovenian youth.
Conducted in the fall of 2020, the survey was part of an awareness campaign called Varni na internetu, targeted at Slovenian adolescents. A total of 3,200 Slovenian adolescents aged 13-19 responded to a comprehensive questionnaire assessing the awareness of 10 online social exploitation scenarios and their personal experiences interacting with these threats.
Results indicate that the majority of respondents were familiar with the described scenarios but a significant minority had never encountered them.
A notable finding is that over 60% of the sampled youth had encountered at least one form of online social exploitation, underscoring the need for continued education and awareness efforts regarding these threats.
Given the alarming prevalence of these threats among the sampled population, it is crucial to foster a culture of online security and responsibility among Slovenian adolescents. To achieve this, educators, parents, and professionals must work together to develop and implement effective online education programs. In the context of data privacy, differential privacy offers robust protection against unauthorized data disclosure. However, optimizing differential private machine learning algorithms often comes at a significant cost, which can compromise the accuracy of the models produced. This research examines the relationship between differential privacy and regularized machine learning. By analyzing the interplay between differential privacy and various regularization techniques, we identify key characteristics of regularizers that facilitate trade-offs between privacy, accuracy, and performance. Specifically, we demonstrate that gradient-based methods can effectively balance privacy, accuracy, and performance. Through a series of experiments, we evaluate the performance of gradient-based methods and other optimization techniques on several datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10. The results show that gradient-based methods can achieve comparable performance to non-private methods, even in scenarios where the noise added to private models would significantly compromise their accuracy. This article examines meromorphic differential functions on $\mathbb{P}^{n}$ that exhibit regular behavior, specifically those which are defined as the quotient of holomorphic functions with well-behaved zeros and holomorphic functions with well-defined poles. We demonstrate that any such function can be expressed as the sum of logarithmic residues associated to holomorphic differential forms on $\mathbb{P}^{n}$. Furthermore, we establish a computational method for calculating these regular meromorphic functions by breaking down the process into a series of determinations of logarithmic residues. We validate the validity of these computations by verifying that the resultant differential forms indeed possess well-defined poles. Additionally, we provide a simplified proof of Saito's residue conjecture, a significant result in the field. Finally, we illustrate the practical application of these methods through a detailed example. We explore and compare the magnetic phase transitions and critical characteristics of the Ising ferromagnet on various lattice structures when subjected to distinct prior measures with equal probability. Segmenting an audio signal into its constituent sound events is a critical task in audio processing.  This task is often tackled using techniques like data clustering or deep learning.  This study presents a new approach, drawing inspiration from object detection techniques, that integrates audio segmentation and sound event detection.  This method uses a real-time, end-to-end trainable neural network architecture, trained on audio recordings with pre-defined event labels.  This training process yields a set of output maps, each containing probability scores for a specific time segment and sound event class.  This output can be interpreted as a segmentation map, labeling different parts of the audio signal with specific sound event probabilities.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in accurately identifying audio segments and sound events and its ability to outperform existing approaches, especially when working with limited training data. By applying our testing framework, we can better understand the benefits and limitations of different methods, which can ultimately lead to more informed decisions about the use of probabilistic fairness methods in practical applications. The intricate dance between color and texture is a longstanding enigma in computer graphics, where color has long been considered the dominant factor and texture the secondary element. However, recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to a reversal of this perspective, revealing that, under certain conditions, it's possible to accurately predict color from texture. This concept is explored in the context of neural noise, where we investigate the relationship between color and texture. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical validation, we've found that neural noise exhibits a unique characteristic: the spatial arrangement of its color information is independent of spatial location. This discovery has significant implications for a range of applications, including the development of a novel color encoding method and the creation of a groundbreaking texture-to-color transfer technique. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of considering the spatial arrangement of color information, which has far-reaching implications for future innovations in computer graphics and vision. Developed by Ecalle, they come with a set of revival monomials that express paralogomials with multiple branch points, offering a comprehensive and efficient way to compute them effectively. This synthesis can be viewed as a type of combinatorial group theory. The resulting method not only streamlines the Ecalle's formula for paralogomials but also has broader applications in computing hyperlogarithms with more complex patterns. Moreover, it can be adapted to calculate resummations of divergent series that fit the same pattern. To overcome the limitations of edge devices in processing Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), we introduce AppealNet, a highly-efficient edge-cloud collaboration framework. AppealNet optimally allocates DNN tasks between edge devices and cloud servers by considering both latency and energy consumption constraints. On the edge, a task partitioning algorithm divides each DNN layer between either local processing or appeal to the cloud for further computation. A novel appeal decision algorithm on the cloud determines which layers to process or appeal further. A layer's decision to appeal is based on a novel metric that considers both local and remote processing costs, taking into account the current device and cloud server loads. Evaluations conducted on a real-world prototype demonstrate AppealNet's ability to significantly reduce inference latency and energy consumption on edge devices. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches, AppealNet showcases superior performance outcomes. For example, in experiments using the YOLOv3 model, AppealNet outperformed the baseline by 23.6% and 17.7% in terms of average latency and energy, respectively. AppealNet also excelled on other models, including YOLOv4, MobilenetV2, SqueezeNet, and ResNet-50. Unlike other theories, the Loops-in-Fabric model generates a spatially flat space in its initial, quantum state rather than a flat space-time. We analyze the time evolution of this model using the Hamilton constraint and demonstrate that spatial geometry becomes classical at all times, while time evolution is represented as a combination of quantum clocks and classical clocks. Furthermore, we establish that the order of these quantum and classical components does not change over time. Notably, the model's predictions for the classical limit match those of General Relativity for all times, including the early universe, and we discuss the implications of these findings for the origins of both quantum and classical reality. Additionally, we explore the broader implications of this model's ability to reconcile quantum and classical spacetime and discuss its potential applications. Finally, we outline possible future directions for exploring the Loops-in-Fabric model.

This study explores strategies to reduce traffic congestion within a hub airport's terminal area, considering multiple public transportation options combined with taxi rides. By modeling passenger traffic using a queueing system, we analyze the effects of two travel methods: a dedicated bus service for airport workers and a financial incentive for delaying departure. The study employs simulation and mathematical analysis to assess the traffic alleviation potential of these options, ultimately finding that increasing the length of departure waits reduces traffic congestion within the airport terminal. Furthermore, offering a financial reward to passengers who wait longer before departing can lead to a significant decrease in traffic congestion. Specifically, doubling the waiting time in the departure area can result in a 9.6% decrease in traffic congestion when a $10 reward is offered for extended waits. This analysis provides insights for airport administrators or developers seeking to mitigate traffic congestion in hub airports by implementing targeted ground transportation strategies. Moreover, this study's findings have broader implications for transportation systems and cities with congestion issues, thanks to the universal applicability of our queueing model. The 2021 FAccT conference marked four years of representing the intersection
of ethics and technology in research. To evaluate the conference's current state
and potential for the future, this paper conducts a mixed-methods analysis,
comparing the 2021 conference to previous years by examining published research,
citation patterns, and submission trends. Our analysis reveals that even as the
spectrum of topics within the community has broadened, research output remains
concentrated on fairness, quantification, and auditing issues. Additionally, we
find that the proportion of technical papers submitted to the conference has
increased, while non-technical papers have remained relatively stable. Our
reflective discussion highlights both opportunities and challenges for the
community to advance in the future, while also outlining potential avenues for
improvement. These include increasing diversity in research output, enhancing
transparency in methodology and findings, and promoting the reproducibility
and generalizability of ethical AI research. Furthermore, we suggest that the
community could benefit from adopting a more inclusive definition of fairness and
exploring the application of fairness to broader social groups. Ultimately, this
paper serves as a starting point for the community to reflect on its current
direction and potential for growth over the next decade. The accompanying
appendix provides additional data and supplementary analyses. This work is
intended to spark further discussion and contribute to the evolution of the
FAccT community, while also promoting the advancement of the ethics research
community as a whole. We hope that the community will join us in shaping the
future of ethics research in technology.

The field of text summarization has become increasingly prominent, with numerous models being developed to achieve this goal. The numerical simulation of wave scattering by obstacles or boundaries poses significant challenges due to numerical noise from infinite layers. In this study, a novel method is presented that eliminates this issue. By introducing a boundary with a specific shape, it is possible to transform infinite layers into finite ones, thereby preventing numerical noise from interfering with wave scattering patterns. Furthermore, this method allows for the exact calculation of finite layer contributions, even when using numerical methods to approximate infinite elements. Performance of the new method was evaluated through numerical simulations of wave scattering by soft and hard obstacles, yielding accurate results that match theoretical expectations. Unlike existing methods, this approach does not introduce errors or exactness at a specific wavenumber, making it a reliable tool for solving wave scattering problems. Its advantages also extend to flexibility in geometry, compatibility with existing solvers, and efficient use of computational resources. By integrating this method into existing tools, it is possible to obtain accurate results with minimal computational costs. In particular, it was shown that the new method can be implemented in the boundary element method to solve two-dimensional wave scattering problems with high accuracy, even when using a limited number of elements. This work is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of wave scattering phenomena and facilitate the development of new numerical tools for solving related problems. To address this, we've developed a new model that incorporates real-time changes in trust in response to moment-to-moment interactions between humans and automation. This model takes into account the immediate impact of automation performance and performance expectations on trust and tested it in a driving simulation experiment. Our results confirm that trust in automation is influenced by both actual outcomes and the expectations that were previously established, and that the relationship between automation performance and trust is not always direct. Specifically, we've found that the relationship between automation performance and trust is not always direct. Rather, it depends on whether the automation's performance meets or falls short of people's expectations, and this relationship can be influenced by various factors, including the automation's performance history and expectations. This model and its implications for designing automated systems for human interaction are also discussed. Ultimately, our research contributes to a better understanding of trust dynamics in automated systems and the complex relationships between human interaction, expectations, and trust. Curriculum learning has been a successful approach to semi-supervised learning, driving advancements in the field.  However, the current methods have limitations in effectively applying it due to their reliance on manual design of the curriculum, and lack of consideration for the quality of the pseudo labels generated at different stages.  In response, we introduce FlexMatch, a flexible semi-supervised learning method that leverages curriculum learning to enhance performance.  FlexMatch employs a dynamic approach to curriculum learning, incrementally increasing the difficulty of the training data as the model improves, using a unique scoring system to assess the model's confidence in its predictions.  Additionally, FlexMatch incorporates a strategy to refine pseudo labels generated at earlier stages, and uses a matching method to filter out low-quality pseudo labels.  Experimental results on the ImageNet-1000 dataset demonstrate that FlexMatch outperforms current state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin, achieving a 12% improvement in accuracy.  The source code for FlexMatch will be made publicly available.  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically address the limitations of existing curriculum learning approaches for semi-supervised learning.  The accompanying experiments and code are unprecedented in their thoroughness and level of detail.  The findings of this work are expected to inspire new research into the field of semi-supervised learning.  All of our code, models, and datasets will be publicly available. A novel approach to machine learning known as Federated Learning (FL) empowers the training process of artificial neural networks on decentralized data without transferring it. This is achieved by training a single model on multiple clients and transferring an updated model to all clients for convergence. FL excels in protecting user privacy, but often yields subpar performance due to its reliance on a unified model. This uniformity can be a limitation, particularly when clients have unique data characteristics. This paper proposes Customized Federated Learning (CFL), which utilizes hypernetworks to tailor each client's model to its distinct data features. In CFL, hypernetworks generate customized models for each client based on their data characteristics. This approach diverges from traditional FL methods that rely on a unified model. Experimental results demonstrate CFL's efficacy in improving performance on clients with unique data and its potential to optimize resource usage. This paper also explores CFL's computational efficiency, demonstrating its potential to expedite the training process. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of CFL's convergence rate reveals its potential to rival existing FL methods. Finally, our research delves into CFL's applicability to non-linear FL scenarios, demonstrating its flexibility and potential to adapt to diverse problem types. Recent studies have revealed that hyperon properties are crucial in modern neutron stars' modeling, particularly in regards to their equation of state. Recent experiments at J-PARC and LHCb have provided new momentum-dependent information about hyperon properties, which is now incorporated into relativistic mean-field models. By analyzing this data, the strength of hyperon potentials in relativistic mean-field models has been adjusted, resulting in a revised interaction within the (anti)hyperon channel. This revised interaction is then applied to neutron stars' modeling, yielding a significant impact on the equation of state, particularly at lower densities, as evidenced by increased neutron star radii and maximum masses. This revised interaction also demonstrates compatibility with GW190814's mass-radius relation, presenting a novel solution to hyperonization's long-standing tension. Furthermore, the effects of isospin-breaking terms on neutron stars' properties are explored, revealing a minimal impact on the equation of state and maximum mass. However, the introduction of isospin-breaking terms does introduce a correlation between the hyperon threshold density and the corresponding binding energy, which is a novel aspect in this context. This revised interaction is now poised to inform future research in this field. For the purposes of public dissemination, the relevant interaction potential parameters are provided in the appendix. Furthermore, the author suggests that future experiments at J-PARC and the LHCbe conducted to measure the hyperon optical potential, which is a necessary step in advancing our understanding of neutron stars' properties. The confluence of the Covid-19 pandemic and July 4th celebrations led to a notable surge in hospitalization rates in New York City, particularly in the months following the outbreak's peak. 

A time-series analysis of EMS events correlated with this increased hospitalization activity revealed a strong connection between EMS transport and inpatient hospital activity. 

Our study developed and evaluated several models to predict EMS events using daily hospitalization trends. 

A model incorporating a deep learning algorithm achieved the best results, providing a potential framework for addressing pandemic-related healthcare demands. 

Our analysis suggests that hospitalization rates and EMS events often move in tandem and are interconnected, making hospitalization data a useful tool in understanding and predicting EMS trends. 
Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the development of strategies for managing pandemic-related healthcare services and emergencies.

To investigate the behavior of polymer chains in solutions, we developed a quantum-mechanical model that simulates their dynamics. By applying this model to short chains of up to ten atoms, we calculated the potential energy landscapes for various configurations. The results indicate that the observed conformations are primarily driven by electrostatic interactions. The study also reveals that as the chain length increases, its conformational space expands significantly. Furthermore, we found that the optimal configuration for a quantum computation, the Bravyi-Kitaev state, exhibits a high potential energy, making it a less favorable choice for this specific task. In contrast, the time-evolved quantum state appears to be a more suitable option. Lastly, we explored the feasibility of computing polymer chemistry using quantum computers by estimating the required quantum resources for specific chemical reactions. The findings suggest that while quantum computing holds promise, current technology still falls short of what's needed to efficiently simulate the behavior of polymer chains in solutions. Nonetheless, there is still room for improvement, and our study provides valuable insights to guide future quantum algorithm development. We develop a powerful non-parametric test for conditional independence in multi-variable analysis that can be efficiently applied to high-dimensional data. This test is built on the principle of the Kullback-Leibler divergence, offering enhanced performance over existing methods like Phillips et al.'s test. Notably, our method excels when dealing with 'phase transitions,' where previous tests struggle, and it also achieves the optimal rejection rate under specific conditions. Furthermore, we illustrate the advantages of the new test through simulations and real-world examples. This research also involves formulating a framework to assess the likelihood of spurious correlations in statistical analysis. By utilizing the conditional independence test, we can establish local rearrangement tests that can detect correlations between subsets of data and individual variables. These tests provide valuable insights into complex relationships in large datasets, where variables often exhibit interdependence. The findings are grounded in the theoretical framework of local sampling distributions. We apply this approach to the analysis of gene expression data, where correlations between gene pairs are influenced by the third variable. This research offers a non-parametric method to identify relationships in high-dimensional data, where assumptions about the distribution of the data are not reliable. This work is an extension of the author's earlier research, presented at the ICML 2022 conference. The new test is implemented in the open-source R package named clrt. This breakthrough leads to a significant equation for generating Bernoulli numbers and highlights the connection between the Hurwitz zeta function and modular forms. Additionally, we derive an innovative representation of Riemann's zeta function as a sum of modular forms and provide a new method for calculating Bernoulli numbers through a non-traditional, modular approach. We also present a new approach to finding the coefficients of the zeta function by linking them to generalized Bernoulli numbers. This work not only builds upon, but also generalizes Ramanujan's and Darmon's contributions to the field. Finally, we explore potential future directions for the application of these findings. This study investigates the potential of C-V2X Mode 4 to handle dense traffic in sub-6 GHz LTE networks during peak hours when a single time slot is insufficient. To enhance network performance, we introduce a dynamic allocation system for multiple sub-6 GHz LTE resources, leveraging knowledge of C-V2X user equipment spatial distributions. Our proposed system allocates dynamic resource sets to each node, maximizing network efficiency. We develop a practical method to select resource candidates and evaluate its impact on C-V2X Mode 4 performance using real-world vehicle tracking data. The results indicate a notable 30% increase in vehicle coverage and 20% rise in safety message delivery rates, achieved through our approach. Our method also shows significant computational savings, requiring only a few percent of the original mode 3 resource selection method's resources. Our work paves the way for future research into more efficient resource management techniques. The code used in this study is publicly available on GitHub. Predicting pedestrian behavior is a critical aspect of autonomous driving, particularly in urban settings where pedestrians are highly interactive. This research focuses on developing a model that can accurately forecast pedestrians' actions by incorporating multiple modalities of data. A novel multi-modal model is proposed, which combines information from a monocular camera, 2D LiDAR camera, and a single RGB-D camera to capture various aspects of a scene. The model's architecture is designed to capture short- and long-term contextual dependencies using convolutional layers, recurrent networks, and a self-attention mechanism. A comprehensive dataset is also created to evaluate the model's performance, which includes 5,500 annotated video clips and 23,500 predicted actions of pedestrians. This dataset is unique in that it provides synchronized data from multiple sensors and accurately labels pedestrians' actions. The proposed model's performance on this dataset is competitive, achieving an F1-score of 0.59 and accuracy of 0.68, with the complete model outperforming a model using a single modality by significant margins. Secure programming relies heavily on secure memory management, which is often overlooked despite its importance. Although secure pointers have been implemented in various programming languages, they typically require manual integration into existing codebases, which can be complex and prone to errors. We introduce Fuel, a compiler-based framework for secure memory management that supports multiple programming languages and formats, making secure coding easier. Unlike other approaches, Fuel uses a different annotation method that's less intrusive and can be applied at runtime. It's also highly versatile, allowing secure pointers to be used across different language boundaries. We've successfully integrated Fuel into Python, Rust, C, and HTML, showing its potential for seamless secure memory management, even in applications that mix different language components. Our evaluation shows that Fuel's performance overhead is minimal and efficient, rivaling the performance of traditional, non-secure implementations, while its memory usage is remarkably close to optimal. We've made Fuel's source code available. Fuel is a testament to the effectiveness of compiler-based frameworks in simplifying secure programming. We introduce Gvnn, a neural network framework rooted in geometric computer vision, where computational processes are defined using geometric transformation languages. Building on the geometric vision literature, this framework enables the representation of a vast array of vision tasks within a common paradigm. By integrating a differentiable solver for these transformation languages, Gvnn facilitates the training of models end-to-end via backpropagation. As a result, the framework empowers the learning of hierarchical image representations, projective camera parameters, and scene geometry from multiple viewpoints, as well as optimization-based vision applications, all through end-to-end training. The framework's versatility is further demonstrated through its application to tasks such as 3D reconstruction, virtual view synthesis, and image denoising, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. The rapid growth of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in data collection, storage, and processing on edge devices, posing potential risks to users. To mitigate these risks, we propose Self-Serviced IoT (SS-IoT), a novel concept that empowers personal cloud creation, enabling users to manage their own IoT infrastructure and regulate data handling from the devices themselves. By giving users complete control, SS-IoT ensures swift and secure offloading of computations, results transfer, and allows users to opt-out at will, thereby maintaining their privacy. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of SS-IoT through its successful implementation on Raspberry Pi 4. For instance, offloading image recognition to personal clouds significantly enhances the system's throughput by up to 115% compared to traditional IoT infrastructure, and achieves an average latency 13% lower than traditional methods. Our findings show that SS-IoT offers substantial benefits over traditional IoT setups and, as an open-source project, we encourage users to join and contribute to the SS-IoT community. Building upon this concept, we also introduce the idea of "Self-Serviced AI" to create a decentralized AI network where AI models are run on edge devices under user-controlled conditions. Our research offers valuable insights into the SS-IoT design space and its potential applications, and we envision its long-term potential to revolutionize IoT and AI development. This letter investigates the performance analysis of a downlink mMTC network powered by a NOMA-based wireless energy collection system, serving multiple multi-user SISO links with random node placements. Focusing on a single-tier architecture, it models the random placement of base stations, energy harvesters, and user equipment as independent Poisson point processes. Employing stochastic geometry, it derives the asymptotic behavior of key system performance metrics such as throughput, delay, and energy efficiency, and showcases the benefits of a carefully designed energy allocation strategy that distinguishes users based on their channel strengths. This approach enables the system to achieve significant gains in system performance, including up to an 300% increase in user throughput and a 3000% increase in user delay energy efficiency. These results highlight the potential of a well-designed energy harvesting system to support a large number of users in mMTC networks. Our method is based on a novel loss function that incorporates a dynamic prior, allowing us to effectively capture the image restoration potential. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in restoring images, and we plan to release our code to the public.

To address this, we've developed a new approach called RAMEN, designed to improve the generalizability of these models. RAMEN achieves this through two key mechanisms: Firstly, it incorporates an additional critic module that's trained alongside the main model, allowing for enhanced boundary representation and more effective domain adaptation. Secondly, RAMEN utilizes an entropy-based technique to identify and emphasize the most challenging questions, facilitating better generalization. Through rigorous testing on the CLEVR dataset, we've found that RAMEN outperforms comparable models by a significant margin, demonstrating its ability to effectively adapt to new and different domains. Our results also show that RAMEN's performance improves as the number of samples from the new domain increases, aligning with expected behavior. Ultimately, these findings suggest that RAMEN holds promise as a powerful tool for visual question answering tasks in diverse, potentially unseen settings. Brain regions communicate through complex, dynamic interactions which can be measured through fMRI BOLD signals. These signals can be analyzed at a detailed voxel level, offering high spatial resolution, or at a regional level, sacrificing spatial precision for improved consistency. This study presents a hybrid approach, integrating regional and voxel-based analysis to estimate functional connections between brain areas. By combining spatial basis functions and regional labels, this approach models the flow of information between brain regions. When applied to resting state fMRI data from the OASIS dataset, the hybrid model demonstrated comparable performance to established methods such as PCA-ICA and dPARS for fMRI connectivity analysis. Notably, it outperformed these models in terms of sensitivity and specificity. This integrated approach, capable of combining spatial and network information, offers a promising framework for understanding how brain regions interact. It has potential applications in analyzing data from other neuroimaging methods, including EEG and MEG. Additional resources and code for this analysis are publicly available on the github repository https://github.com/umlaamr/region_bond. This integrated approach offers a valuable tool for analyzing fMRI data and may contribute to a deeper understanding of brain function.

This alternative method involves a two-step process, first estimating the flow of information between voxels and then aggregating this information to form a network of brain regions. The performance of this approach was evaluated using the same dataset and metrics as the original study, yielding results that were comparable to those achieved with the hybrid model presented in the original paper. Notably, the original spatial basis-based model demonstrated higher sensitivity and specificity than the alternative method. In contrast, the alternative method exhibited comparable performance to the other approaches, including PCA-ICA and dPARS. Overall, the alternative method offers a viable alternative for analyzing fMRI data at both voxel and regional levels. Its performance suggests that the flow of information between voxels and between brain regions is closely linked. This finding has important implications for understanding how brain regions interact and may contribute to a deeper understanding of this complex process.

Music streaming services have become a crucial aspect of our daily lives, 
integrated into our mobile devices to effortlessly access music playlists at any time. 
The mobile interface's design, with its layout and function placement, is intended to 
stimulate user interaction, yet the dynamics of this interaction remain unclear. 
This study employs eye-tracking technology to investigate users' natural behaviors 
when interacting with music streaming services, specifically exploring how music 
tracks are visually selected. Our findings indicate that users tend to focus on the 
track's name, while also examining the artist name, although this attention varies 
across different platforms. Additionally, we discovered that users' selection behaviors 
are influenced by the placement of the play button within the interface. These insights 
should inform the development of music streaming interfaces to enhance user 
convenience and experience.

A quantum system connected to a bath at thermal equilibrium exhibits behavior
defined by the von Neumann entropy, a key characteristic. This study examines
the influence of a non-extensive quantum system connected to a thermal bath in a
variety of scenarios. By analyzing the dynamics of the Renyi entropy across
different systems, we identify distinct patterns in their evolution. Furthermore, 
the Lindblad spectrum is investigated as a measure, revealing connections to 
the Renyi entropy and demonstrating that its spectrum mirrors the system's 
entropic evolution, aligns with the system's eigenstates, and correlates with 
the subsystem's subentropy. This research also explores the potential for 
experimental verification within the context of the ultrastrong coupling regime. 
The findings are substantiated through numerical simulations of the Dicke model. 
Our study provides a deeper understanding of the behavior of quantum systems 
connected to baths and may inspire new insights into the interplay between 
entanglement and thermalization in quantum systems. Additionally, 
the proposed measurement of the Lindblad spectrum offers a valuable tool for 
investigating and characterizing the system's behavior. This research has been 
published in a recent issue of Physical Review E.  The research team suggests

entropic behavior of quantum systems connected to baths and may also have

Research has shown that pre-trained language models can introduce biases into downstream neural machine translation tasks. This bias stems from semantic divergences between source and target languages in the model's vocabulary, which can lead to incorrect translations due to word meanings, their grammatical contexts, and discourse contexts. To address this, we developed a method that utilizes the similarity between words in the model's vocabulary, using perplexity scores to guide the editing of translations in specific situations where semantic divergences are most pronounced. This approach is based on the idea that words with similar meanings in the model should be interchangeable in translation, and we tested its effectiveness on a range of datasets in different languages. Our results show that this method can significantly improve translation quality, particularly in situations where semantic divergences are most damaging, while also maintaining efficiency. This approach can be used in conjunction with other methods to post-edit translations and to identify areas where semantic editing is most needed. Our results demonstrate the potential for semantic editing to improve translation quality, and we make our code available to facilitate further research in this area. This includes the pre-trained language models used for semantic editing, as well as the evaluation datasets and code for the editing process. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyu-dvlpmnt/sem-edits. It uses iterative iterative multivariate regression to predict missing values. In this study, we explore how modifying the multivariate regression component of MICE can improve the process. Our approach involves replacing multivariate regression with principal component regression, and we also investigated using a combination of both, referred to as principal component chaining. To assess the effectiveness of these methods, we conducted a simulation study and found that modifying the multivariate regression process led to improved accuracy. Specifically, we found that PCA-chaining performed better than the other approaches, achieving the best results, although PCA-chaining resulted in a slightly increased computational time. Furthermore, we applied PCA-chaining to a real-world dataset and the results were found to be consistent with the simulated data. Overall, our study demonstrates that modifying the multivariate regression component of MICE can be a useful strategy. By applying a general expansion based on the distribution of density modes, the theory yields an expression that can be decomposed into two distinct components: one accounting for interactions and another accounting for shape asymmetry. By leveraging the inherent properties of the underlying density modes, the method circumvents the complexities associated with the more traditional route of solving for the density modes within the grand potential. Furthermore, the theory's formulation facilitates the derivation of explicit equations for both the fluid's total grand potential and the fluid's equilibrium density profile. Notably, this framework is well-suited for the analysis of thin films and curved surfaces. Additionally, the theory's versatility has been demonstrated through its ability to incorporate various shape parameters, including those related to ellipsoids and hard spherocylinders. Finally, the method's accuracy has been validated through a series of numerical simulations and comparisons with existing literature results. The presence of simultaneous conversation significantly hampers the identification of speakers within audio recordings and speech-to-text systems. To address this issue, researchers have developed various approaches, such as speech enhancement and separation, which are often paired with cutting-edge language models. Our research builds upon recent advancements in automatic speech recognition and introduces a straightforward method for detecting gender using the WavLM pre-trained transformer. Notably, WavLM has been employed for a range of speech-related tasks, including speaker recognition, language models, and text generation. Our proposed system leverages the WavLM's contextualized representation to identify gender while utilizing the audio encoder's embeddings for speaker identification. This approach is demonstrated to be effective in both cases, with our results showing comparable performance to state-of-the-art benchmarks. Our method also offers the advantage of being less computationally demanding, making it a viable option for real-world applications. Reinforcement learning has been instrumental in developing intelligent agents that excel at complex tasks, but most existing methods focus on maximizing a single, long-term goal at a given state. In contrast, many real-world tasks involve achieving multiple, interconnected objectives. To tackle such multi-objective tasks, a novel approach called Temporal Transition Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) is proposed, which focuses on learning the optimal transitions between different states to maximize a dynamic reward. TTRL is demonstrated to be effective in addressing multi-stage tasks, where agents aim to achieve a series of interconnected objectives. To validate the efficacy of this approach, a detailed implementation is provided, and the proposed method is successfully applied to a multi-stage benchmark task involving a humanoid robot, showcasing its ability to learn complex transitions and achieve the desired goals. Furthermore, the performance of TTRL is compared to a state-based baseline, revealing its superior adaptability in handling complex multi-stage tasks. Additionally, the code and datasets developed for this research are made available for public access. The research findings suggest that TTRL offers a promising solution for learning optimal transitions in complex, multi-objective tasks, and the code can be found at https://github.com/RoboticsAdvocate/TTRL. but they often describe the same fundamental phenomena. We demonstrate that 
the diverse representation types in these fields are actually expressions of the 
same underlying Hilbert-Space framework. By applying unification principles, 
we can translate and unify concepts between the two theories without altering 
their fundamental meaning. This unification enables us to explore novel 
quantum phenomena through a unified mathematical approach. We apply this 
framework to study the ground state and excitation spectrum of a general 
quantum spin model, using the Holstein-Primakoff transformation, and examine 
its application in both Condensed Matter Science and Quantum Field Theory. 
The results reveal a deeper connection between the two theories and open up new 
areas of research for investigation. This work may inspire further studies on 
developing a unified understanding of quantum systems, which could facilitate 
research into emerging phenomena in quantum technology. Ultimately, this 
unification paves the way for a deeper connection between Condensed Matter Science 
and Quantum Field Theory, and we envision its potential for advancing 
understanding of quantum systems, as well as their applications in quantum

Notably, the method can generate a range of object possibilities, exceeding the number of labeled instances for a particular object category. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly impacted the world, causing widespread loss of life, economic devastation, and disruption to numerous sectors. Despite its far-reaching consequences, the pandemic's influence on scientific research has received relatively little attention. This study examines the effects of the pandemic on scientific discovery in the life sciences, leveraging a vast database of over 100,000 academic papers related to COVID-19. Our analysis reveals that the pandemic has accelerated the pace of scientific innovation, with the distribution of publication times exhibiting a distinct, asymmetrical pattern. Furthermore, we have identified and quantified the key factors contributing to this phenomenon, including the impact of social distancing and the role of scientific anticipation in research production. Our findings also suggest that the pandemic has facilitated the identification of emerging research opportunities, with the 'burst block' period following the initial surge in publication activity seen in various scientific indices. The implications of these discoveries are discussed in relation to the long-term potential of scientific research to mitigate the effects of future pandemics. Additionally, we propose that the analysis of publication patterns can serve as an early warning system for future health crises, thus enabling proactive preparation and mitigation strategies. Ultimately, the insights gained from this study can inform the development of more effective policies aimed at enhancing scientific research and reducing the burden of future public health emergencies. A novel framework, ENOS, has been proposed for Energy-aware Neural Operator Search. This framework optimizes the energy usage of neural operators on hybrid accelerators that combine digital and compute-in-memory components. ENOS employs a two-stage strategy, initially searching for the optimal combination of digital and compute-in-memory operators at a lower energy cost, and subsequently fine-tuning the digital operator's precision to minimize energy. ENOS allows for flexible tradeoffs between energy and performance, and achieves significant improvements in energy efficiency, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks. For instance, it achieves 2.8$\times$ better energy efficiency, and 2.1$\times$ lower energy consumption, than the best existing approach. ENOS can accelerate neural network inference by 2.2$\times$, and has been successfully implemented on a cutting-edge accelerator card. Its source code is available online.

We analyze the discrepancy between the solution of a stochastic differential equation with jumps and its Gaussian approximation, measured by the total variation distance in space over time. Given the non-local nature of the operator appearing in the equation, we prove that its solution is Lipschitz continuous in time and has finite total variation, thus establishing a bound on the distance between these two solutions. Furthermore, we derive an asymptotic formula describing the behavior of the distance as the jump size approaches zero.
The key technical challenge lies in estimating the contribution of small-scale jumps that result in an infinite number of small jumps at any fixed time point. Our approach to resolving this issue involves a novel method of decomposing the distance into the sum of two terms: the first term represents the distance between solutions of two related jump times, while the second term represents the cumulative effect of jumps occurring between these points of interest. By analyzing these two components separately, we are able to establish the desired bounds on the distance. Our results are applicable to a broad class of jump-dispersion equations and can be applied to a variety of practical problems involving the approximation of stochastic processes. Additionally, our work provides a general framework for studying the approximation of stochastic processes and can be used to establish a general bound on the distance between solutions of stochastic equations. As a special case, we prove that the distance between solutions of the celebrated Black-Scholes equation and its local approximation is bounded by the jump size, measured in total variation distance. This result is then used to derive an asymptotic expansion of the local approximation, valid up to the second order of the jump size. Our work is motivated by the practical need to develop a numerical scheme for approximating the solution of the Black-Scholes equation. Given the non-local nature of the operator appearing in this equation, we are faced with the technical challenge of estimating the distance between the solution of the original equation and its local approximation, a problem that has not been addressed in the existing literature. Our results provide a solution to this problem, allowing us to derive a numerical scheme for approximating the solution of the Black-Scholes equation. This scheme can be used to estimate the value of European-style options, measured by their intrinsic or option pricing (Bachelier) volatility. By applying our results to this specific problem, we are able to derive a numerical scheme for approximating the solution of the Black-Scholes equation, and our work is the first to provide a general framework for studying the approximation of stochastic processes and the derivation of asymptotic expansions of their solutions.
